meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('rare, scarce, unusual').

examples.text: У меня есть много редких материалов.
examples.trans: I have many rare materials.

examples.text: Макс, почему редкие трюфели оказались на помойке?
examples.trans: Max, why did rare truffles end up in the dumpster?

examples.text: Но вы обязаны распробовать этот редкий шедевр!
examples.trans: But you must taste this rare masterpiece!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лучай'). Common masculine noun meaning 'case, occasion, incident' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Take it, just in case.
This is a strange case.

examples.text: Возьмите, пожалуйста. На случай, если передумаете.
examples.trans: Please take this. In case you change your mind.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'when', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: When I grow up, I'll be the mayor.
Oh yeah? When?

examples.text: Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
examples.trans: When I grow up, you'll be begging me to forgive you!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тарик'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'old man' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This old man is sitting on the bench.
The old man told an interesting story.

examples.text: Я не могу спать спокойно! Этот старик крадёт у девушки лучшие годы.
examples.trans: I cannot sleep in peace! This old man is stealing the girl's best years.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('right').

examples.text: Заходите. Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Come in. Please put your right foot on the bed.

examples.text: Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Please put your right foot on the bed.

examples.text: Я тебя обманул, и ты был прав. Теперь всё изменилось, Самсон.
examples.trans: I tricked you, and you were right. Now everything has changed, Samson.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

надоесть.gloss: to bore, to get on someone's nerves

meanings.en: to bore, to get on someone's nerves
meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'доесть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to bore, to get on someone's nerves', paired with 'надоедать'.

related.gloss: not to got tired of (negated infinitive)

examples.trans: I'm tired of waiting.
I'm sick of you!

examples.text: Надоело мне в этом архиве сидеть.
examples.trans: I'm tired of sitting in this archive.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from; of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: A letter from Mum.
I'm tired of work.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'which, who', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

examples.text: Чтобы он вернул деньги, которые украл.
examples.trans: For him to give back the money he stole.

examples.text: Который ему город подарил! И откуда у Аллы Евгеньевны новая шуба!
examples.trans: Which the city donated to him! And where Alla Yevgenyevna got a new fur coat!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'традать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to suffer', paired with 'пострадать'.

examples.trans: He is supposed to suffer.
People are suffering because of him.

examples.text: Ну и что? Он должен страдать, а нам нужна информация.
examples.trans: So what? He is supposed to suffer, and we need the information.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
As you all know...
Share with everyone.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'staff, personnel' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is a delicious lunch for the staff.

examples.text: Сегодня обед для персонала готовит наш огузок.
examples.trans: Today our runt is cooking lunch for the staff.

examples.text: Тогда иди быстрее в раздевалку персонала.
examples.trans: Then go faster to the staff locker room.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'нять'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to understand', paired with 'понимать'.

examples.trans: I didn't understand.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?
I understand you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'what; what a', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What is your town like?
What a beautiful house!

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'war' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Read The Art of War, by Sun Tzu!
This book tells about the war.

examples.text: В прошлый раз я думала, война началась.
examples.trans: Last time I thought a war had started.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Common Russian noun meaning 'kids; guys' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Тогда ребята с тобой поработают. До свидания, Аркадий Борисович.
examples.trans: Then the boys will have a little word with you. Goodbye, Arkady Borisovich.
Then the boys will have a little word with you.
Right, kids, go out of the room.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to be enough', paired with 'хватать'.

examples.trans: There wasn't enough money.
Gum? I didn't have enough money.
Enough, enough!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to mean'.

examples.trans: What does this mean?
So you're not coming.
Pasha, what does all this mean?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'more; still; yet', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You've still got some.
You'll be sorry!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'time, occasion' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Just once.
Say it once more.
What do you mean, once?

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ращаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to right'.

examples.text: Ты как к су-шефу обращаешься сейчас?
examples.trans: How are you addressing the sous-chef right now?

examples.text: Уважаемые коллеги, прошу минуточку вашего внимания!
examples.trans: Dear colleagues, I ask for a minute of your attention!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'to, towards', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.
I'm going to Mum's.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

потрудиться.gloss: to take the trouble, to bother

meanings.en: to take the trouble, to bother
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'трудиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to take the trouble, to bother', paired with 'трудиться'.

examples.trans: Kindly do not bother me anymore!
He worked hard.

examples.text: Я ничего не защемила! Потрудитесь меня больше не беспокоить!
examples.trans: I didn't pinch anything! Kindly don't bother me anymore!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: What are you doing?
I'm making dinner.
Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'so that, in order to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So that there are witnesses.
I'm calling to say thank you.
So that there are witnesses, Samson.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'cook, chef' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There is this English chef.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'wander'.

related.gloss: not to you wander around (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Ты считаешь, что можешь шляться где угодно?
examples.trans: You think you can wander off anywhere?

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и шляться вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and you wander around on time.
Where have you been wandering around so long?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'along; by; about', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm here about the job.
We're talking on the phone.

examples.text: Это Аракелян. Я по поводу торгового центра.
examples.trans: It's Arakelyan. I'm calling about the shopping centre.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'hall, large room; courtroom' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Please enter the courtroom.
A big hall.
Understood. And who is managing the dining room?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

выйти.gloss: to go out, to get out

meanings.en: to go out, to get out
meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to go out, to get out', paired with 'выходить'.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks.
He left the house.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели. Я решу все ваши проблемы.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks. I'll solve all your problems.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from, out of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The town hall called me.
He's from Moscow.

examples.text: Марина Сергеевна, я уже знаю. Мне звонили из мэрии.
examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna, I already know. The town hall called me.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I feel good.
He only thinks about himself.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

examples.text: А если я не скажу, то что? Ты мне ухо отрежешь?
examples.trans: And if I don't tell you, then what? Will you cut my ear off?

examples.text: А если я не скажу, то что?
examples.trans: And if I don't tell you, then what?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('necessary, needed').

examples.trans: I need a job too.
Do you need a pen?
He needs money.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'such, like this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What is this?
He's so kind.
Pavel Yuryevich, what is this?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, by; (у меня) I have', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
He's at our place.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ильный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strong, powerful').

examples.text: Сильный ищет способ, а слабый ищет причину.
examples.trans: The strong man looks for a way, and the weak man looks for an excuse.
A strong wind was blowing outside.

examples.text: Надо заманить его на свою территорию. Там, где ты сильный.
examples.trans: You need to lure him onto your territory. Right where you are strong.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'жный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('gentle, tender, delicate').

examples.text: Я могу быть очень нежным и ласковым.
examples.trans: I can be very gentle and affectionate.

examples.text: Марина, я могу быть очень нежным и ласковым.
examples.trans: Marina, I can be very gentle and affectionate.

examples.text: Тогда наше мясо будет намного нежнее.
examples.trans: Then our meat will be much more tender.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'hand; arm' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Give me your hand.
I shake your hand! (a goodbye)
Right, cheers then.
